cases.title: Hotel customer segmentation
cases.imageAlt: Illustration of the Da Nang coastline and hotels
cases.lead: Guest reviews reveal different priorities within the same hotel market. This study grouped Da Nang guests by the service attributes they discussed and how they rated them.
cases.question: What do different guests value?
cases.study: Overall ratings can hide differences between guests. Review text was mapped to hotel attributes, scored for sentiment and grouped with K-means. A Gaussian mixture model provided a robustness check.
cases.findingTitle: Ten groups within the review data
cases.finding: The largest reported group, Minimalists, accounts for 43.7% of the sample. Smaller groups focus on dining, exploration, service and other parts of the stay.
cases.use: The segmentation gives hotel teams a way to compare guest priorities before choosing service improvements or messages for different audiences.
cases.limit: Segments describe the review sample. Their shares should not be treated as hotel occupancy, market share or measured revenue effects.

visual.title: Guest groups
visual.caption: Reported share of the review sample. Select a group to compare its size.

notes: Dataset
Project materials report 74,896 Booking.com reviews across 458 Da Nang hotels. This is the dataset for this segmentation study.
Analysis
Attribute-level sentiment analysis (ABSA), K-means clustering and a Gaussian mixture robustness check. The materials report 108,906 sentences and 148,846 extracted aspect–sentence pairs.
Evidence
Dataset counts and segment shares are reported in the project materials; they have not been independently verified here.

cases.title: EV choice experiment
cases.imageAlt: Illustration of an electric vehicle at a city charging point
cases.lead: A choice experiment with young consumers in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City examined how range, charging, network size and body design affect EV preferences.
cases.question: Which trade-offs shape an EV choice?
cases.study: Participants compared vehicle profiles with different features. Multinomial and mixed logit models were compared with a latent class model to examine differences between buyer groups.
cases.findingTitle: Two ways to value an EV
cases.finding: The reported model separates a utility-focused group (65%) from a design-sensitive group (35%). Range has the highest marginal willingness-to-pay estimate in both groups. Design estimates are less certain.
cases.use: The results can inform product positioning and the features emphasized for each group. They do not establish demand at a particular retail price.
cases.limit: These are stated preferences and model estimates. Several attribute confidence intervals include zero; the estimated willingness to pay is not a sales result.

visual.title: Compare the two groups
visual.caption: Marginal willingness to pay, VND million per attribute change. Reported model estimates.

states.label: Utility-focused · 65%
states.note: The larger group places most of its estimated value on driving range.

states.label: Design-sensitive · 35%
states.note: Estimates are higher in this group, but the design interval still includes zero.

notes: Sample and model
212 validated young consumers in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City. Reported two-class split: 65% / 35%; model log-likelihood: −1523.26.
Uncertainty

Utility-focused 95% intervals: range 65.3–202.5; charging −6.7–198.7; network −26.4–113.8; body −21.8–108.4. Design-sensitive intervals: range 100.2–259.8; charging 19.4–191.2; network 21.8–99.2; body −24.8–160.7. Units match the figure.
Status
CIEMB manuscript/conference context. The current materials do not establish an external publication record or measured commercial outcomes.

cases.title: Virtual influencers and purchase intention
cases.imageAlt: Illustrative portrait of a virtual influencer
cases.lead: A survey experiment tested whether the message or the virtual creator's appeal affected purchase intention among Vietnamese Generation Z consumers.
cases.question: Does the message or the creator persuade?
cases.study: Participants saw one of four simulated Instagram posts. The experiment varied argument quality and peripheral appeal, then examined purchase intention and the moderating role of speciesism.
cases.findingTitle: Creator appeal mattered, with a limit
cases.finding: Peripheral cues could affect purchase intention independently. Participants with stronger preferences for human endorsers reported lower purchase intention regardless of the virtual creator's attractiveness.
cases.use: The result supports examining audience acceptance alongside creator design. Attractive visuals alone may not persuade audiences who strongly prefer human endorsers.
cases.limit: The experiment measured purchase intention after simulated content exposure. It did not measure purchases or campaign conversion.

visual.title: The four experimental conditions
visual.caption: Argument quality and peripheral appeal were varied separately. Select a condition to view its stimulus.

items.label: Strong argument · high appeal
items.note: Both the product argument and peripheral creator cues were strengthened.

items.label: Weak argument · high appeal
items.note: Peripheral creator cues were strengthened while the product argument was weaker.

items.label: Strong argument · low appeal
items.note: The product argument was strengthened while peripheral creator cues were weaker.

items.label: Weak argument · low appeal
items.note: Both dimensions were presented at their lower experimental levels.

notes: Framework
Elaboration likelihood model: argument quality represents the central route; social attractiveness, physical attractiveness and attitude similarity represent peripheral cues.
Speciesism
The study uses speciesism to examine stronger preferences for human over non-human endorsers. It is a moderator, not an additional experimental condition.
Publication

Exploring the Effect of Social Media Content of Virtual Influencers on Generation Z’s Purchase Intention: An Elaboration Likelihood Model Approach. Springer Proceedings in Business and Economics, pages 143–157. DOI 10.1007/978-981-96-4116-1_9.

cases.title: Student diet quality
cases.imageAlt: Illustration of a university student and a balanced meal
cases.lead: A survey of 280 university students examined nutrition knowledge, physical activity and the foods eaten on the previous day.
cases.question: How does knowledge relate to daily food choices?
cases.study: The study combined a 20-item nutrition knowledge scale, physical activity measures and a dietary questionnaire. Regression examined their associations with diet quality while accounting for age and sex.
cases.finding: Students answered basic dietary questions more accurately than calorie questions. The reported diet scores also showed more foods to limit than protective food groups.
cases.use: The findings suggest specific topics for nutrition education and areas to examine in campus food provision. Physical activity was associated with better diet quality in the regression.
cases.limit: A cross-sectional survey identifies associations. It does not show that an education or activity programme caused better diets.

visual.title: Knowledge and dietary patterns
visual.caption: Values reproduced from the paper. Dietary averages use different maximum scores and should not be read as percentages.

states.label: Knowledge
states.note: Correct answers by knowledge domain, Table 2.

states.label: Dietary pattern
states.note: Reported means: diversity 6.1/10, protective groups 3.9/9 and foods to limit 6.1/12.

notes: Instruments
Adapted CoNKS: 20 items. IPAQ-SF: activity in MET-minutes per week. DQQ: 29 food groups with food-diversity and Global Dietary Recommendations scores.
Regression
The reported model explains 53.8% of the variance in the diet-quality score (R² = 0.538). Physical activity, age and nutrition knowledge have positive adjusted associations; sex is not significant.
Source
Values were checked against the hosted FCBEM paper, including Tables 2 and 3. The results describe this student sample rather than all Vietnamese students.

cases.title: Motorbike phase-out policy
cases.imageAlt: Hanoi metro train as an alternative to motorcycle travel
cases.lead: A policy choice study examined how Hanoi residents valued travel restrictions, public transport improvements and support for changing vehicles.
cases.question: What makes a transition acceptable?
cases.study: Participants evaluated policy packages. The model estimated how restrictions and support measures changed their choices, with willingness to pay expressed in VND per month.
cases.findingTitle: Restrictions and support pull in different directions
cases.finding: Restrictions on fossil-fuel vehicles carried negative willingness-to-pay estimates. Public transport improvements, reinvestment and an electric-motorcycle grant carried positive estimates.
cases.use: The study supports comparing support measures alongside restrictions when discussing a transition package. The estimates describe stated policy preferences.
cases.limit: The model does not forecast traffic, compliance or the outcome of a particular regulation. The sequencing proposal remains a policy interpretation.

visual.title: Monthly willingness to pay
visual.caption: Selected values from the reported manuscript tables. A negative value indicates compensation needed; a positive value indicates support for the attribute.

states.label: Restrictions
states.note: Reported restrictions carry negative values in the choice model.

states.label: Support measures
states.note: Reported support values are positive. They are model estimates, not policy budgets.

notes: Model
The project materials report n = 320, ρ² = 0.28 and an alternative-specific constant of +1.621. The figure uses values from manuscript Tables 4 and 5.
Interpretation
Greater dependence on motorcycles changes how restrictions are valued. Income, environmental concern and trust also appear in the reported interaction analysis.
Status
CIEMB manuscript/conference context. Existing portfolio figures report the model values; no external publication record is established here.

cases.title: Hotel service priorities
cases.imageAlt: Illustration of a hotel resort and guest facilities
cases.lead: An analysis of hotel reviews examined whether poor service and good service had equal effects on review scores.
cases.question: Which service failures cost the most?
cases.study: Review text was mapped to eight attributes with Sentence-BERT. Positive and negative sentiment indicators entered a regression to compare reward and penalty coefficients.
cases.findingTitle: Cleanliness and staff service have different roles
cases.finding: Cleanliness has the largest reported penalty when it fails. Staff service has the largest positive reward coefficient. The model groups attributes into basic, performance and excitement categories.
cases.use: Hotel teams can use the comparison to distinguish failures that need attention from improvements that may support differentiation.
cases.limit: Regression coefficients describe associations with review scores. They do not establish the revenue return from investing in an attribute.

visual.title: Penalty and reward by attribute
visual.caption: Reported regression coefficients. Compare the downside of negative sentiment with the upside of positive sentiment.

states.label: Penalty
states.note: Cleanliness has the largest negative coefficient.

states.label: Reward
states.note: Staff service has the largest positive reward coefficient; the WiFi estimate remains negative.

notes: Dataset
The project materials report 97,014 Booking.com reviews from approximately 1,000 Vietnamese properties, collected for Jan 2023–Jan 2025.
Model
Robust regression with HC1 standard errors; R² = 0.220. Mean review score: 8.83/10. Eight service attributes were classified.
Classification
Basic: cleanliness and WiFi. Performance: staff, room quality, value and location. Excitement: facilities and food.

cases.title: Hotel customer value
cases.imageAlt: Illustration of a hotel breakfast and service experience
cases.lead: This framework translates themes in guest reviews into service priorities that hotel teams can discuss and test.
cases.question: How can review themes guide a service decision?
cases.study: Review themes are mapped to value dimensions such as comfort, service care and local experience. Guest stories then connect those themes with possible service and messaging choices.
cases.findingTitle: Three ways to discuss guest value
cases.finding: Comfort seekers, local experience hunters and reliability-first travelers represent different service priorities. These are communication profiles for the framework, not additional measured segments.
cases.use: A hotel team can select a profile, review its priorities and use it as a starting point for a service-design discussion.
cases.limit: The profiles and actions are conceptual. Dataset counts and measured segment shares belong to the linked segmentation study.

visual.title: Compare guest priorities
visual.caption: Conceptual profiles for interpreting review themes. No market shares or measured effects are assigned.

items.label: Relaxed comfort
items.title: Rest and comfort
items.note: Room comfort, calm ambience and attentive service are the main priorities in this profile.

items.label: Local experience
items.title: Food and discovery
items.note: Local food, recommendations and access to nearby experiences shape the service discussion.

items.label: Reliable stay
items.title: Predictable service
items.note: Convenient access, responsive staff and consistent room quality guide the discussion.

notes: Relationship to the study
This is an interpretation layer for the Da Nang segmentation work. It does not introduce an independent dataset.
Value dimensions
Comfort, service care, local food, location ease, ambience and overall value provide the framework vocabulary.
Evidence
The profiles summarize proposed service priorities. The framework does not establish numerical importance weights.

cases.title: Influencer engagement and retention
cases.imageAlt: Illustration of creator content and audience interaction
cases.lead: A survey of active UGC-platform users examined how content experience, expectation alignment and brand equity relate to engagement and retention.
cases.question: What sits between exposure and returning?
cases.study: The sample was split between exploratory factor analysis and confirmatory measurement and structural analysis. The model tested engagement as the pathway linking the antecedent constructs with retention.
cases.finding: The reported model explains 55% of engagement variance and 70% of retention variance. These are explanatory statistics, not increases in engagement or customer retention.
cases.use: The model suggests examining content quality, expectation matching and creator–brand fit alongside the depth of audience interaction.
cases.limit: The cross-sectional survey does not prove that changing a campaign causes customers to return. Available materials do not include a complete public coefficient table.

visual.title: The reported model structure
visual.caption: Select an input to follow its path through engagement. The diagram shows relationships, not measured conversion uplift.

items.label: Content experience
items.note: Informational and narrative quality of creator content enters the model through engagement.

items.label: Expectation alignment
items.note: The match between creator claims and the delivered experience enters the model through engagement.

items.label: Brand equity
items.note: Creator credibility and brand associations enter the model through engagement.

notes: Sample
565 active UGC users in Vietnam. Exploratory factor analysis used 200 respondents; CFA and SEM used 365. Exact collection dates are not available in the current source set.
Constructs
CX: content experience. CEX: expectation alignment. BE: brand equity transfer. CE: consumer engagement. CR: customer retention.
Source boundary
The source contains archived manuscript screenshots and reported model structure. External creator examples were explanatory cases, not survey observations, and are omitted from this concise page.

cases.title: Buffet menu choices
cases.imageAlt: Hotpot buffet meal used to illustrate the study context
cases.lead: Two studies tested how the order of menu information affected intended calorie intake, perceived value and the choice of a higher-priced buffet tier.
cases.question: Does menu order change a diner's choice?
cases.study: Participants saw menu conditions with healthier options or price tiers presented in different orders. The analysis compared intended intake and estimated the odds of choosing a higher tier.
cases.findingTitle: Lower intended intake came with a trade-off
cases.finding: Healthier-first menus reduced intended calorie intake in both studies. In Study 2, the reported premium-tier choice share fell from 52.4% to 23.8%.
cases.use: The result gives operators a menu-order option to test, while showing why perceived value and premium-tier demand need to be considered together.
cases.limit: The studies measured stated choices and intended intake. They did not measure plate waste in an operating restaurant.

visual.title: Compare the menu conditions
visual.caption: Reported mean intended calorie intake. These are intentions measured in the study, not observed food consumption.

states.label: Unhealthy options first
states.note: Reported means in the comparison condition.

states.label: Healthier options first
states.note: Intended intake is lower by 146 kcal in Study 1 and 223 kcal in Study 2.

notes: Study design
Study 1: buffet/hotpot choice experiment, n = 257. Study 2: price-tier choice experiment, n = 147. The source describes a 2 × 3 between-subjects design and ordinal logistic analysis.
Tier choice
Higher-tier odds ratio: 0.52, meaning 48% lower odds, not a 48-point decrease in probability. Premium choice share changes from 52.4% to 23.8%.
Mediation
Reported indirect effect through perceived value: −0.339, 95% CI [−0.56, −0.15]. This helps interpret the commercial trade-off in the experimental conditions.

cases.title: Psychological ownership at university
cases.imageAlt: Illustration of a university setting and shared work
cases.lead: This framework examines how a sense that work is mine or ours may relate to commitment and cooperation in universities.
cases.question: How does ownership relate to commitment?
cases.study: The framework connects control over work, identification with it and shared responsibility with organizational commitment. It outlines relationships to examine rather than reporting a new university dataset.
cases.finding: Individual ownership concerns a person's connection with the work. Collective ownership concerns a shared sense of responsibility. Both provide questions for examining commitment and teamwork.
cases.use: Universities can use the framework to frame interviews or future surveys about participation in decisions, the meaning of work and shared goals.
cases.limit: The current materials do not provide a study sample, model fit or university-specific effect sizes. The pathway is conceptual.

visual.title: Explore the proposed relationships
visual.caption: Conceptual diagram. Select a perspective to see the relationship it proposes.

items.label: Individual ownership
items.note: A personal sense of connection, influence and identification with work may relate to commitment.

items.label: Collective ownership
items.note: A shared sense of responsibility may relate to commitment and cooperation.

notes: Definition
Psychological ownership refers to a felt connection with a target such as work or an organization. It is distinct from legal ownership.
Evidence gap
The current portfolio sources do not include a sample, university-specific coefficients or confirmed SEM results.
Practical reading
Use the framework to define research questions. Outcomes such as improved teaching or employee retention require separate evidence.

cases.title: Arts workshop participation
cases.imageAlt: Research team in the arts workshop setting
cases.lead: A survey at Ladder Art Space examined how learning, social and enjoyment values related to attitudes toward a workshop and intentions to participate.
cases.question: What makes a workshop worth joining?
cases.study: The analysis examined experience values, workshop attitude and participation intention. Measurement checks and PROCESS Model 4 were used to examine the mediation pathway.
cases.finding: The project materials report learning value as the strongest signal for attitude. The reported paths are 0.35 from learning value to attitude and 0.59 from attitude to intention.
cases.use: The findings suggest testing clear learning goals, beginner guidance and feedback during the workshop. These are service-design proposals rather than measured attendance gains.
cases.limit: The cross-sectional data measures intention. It does not prove that these changes cause bookings or repeat attendance.

visual.title: From experience to participation intention
visual.caption: Reported pathway and service-design interpretation. Select an experience value to follow its role.

items.label: Learning value
items.note: Reported learning-value → attitude path: 0.35. Participants valued what they could learn to make.

items.label: Social value
items.note: The model examines social value alongside the other experience dimensions. A separate numeric path is not assigned here.

items.label: Enjoyment
items.note: The model examines enjoyment alongside learning and social value. A separate numeric path is not assigned here.

notes: Sample and setting
216 valid responses after screening; Ladder Art Space, Melbourne. Figures are reported in the project page.
Analysis
Measurement checks, structural paths and PROCESS Model 4. The current source set does not provide enough detail to label the displayed coefficients as standardized or causal.
Evidence
The sample and paths are reported in the project materials. A publication record and independent data verification are not provided.
